newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland must brace for rain, new floods, PM says.
newsitem.headline: Poland must brace for rain, new floods, PM says.

text.p: Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz warned on Thursday that forecast heavy rains could trigger another wave of the disastrous flooding that has already killed 46 people and swamped huge areas of the country.
So severe have been the floods that Poland's currency and stock market have been hit and opposition parties are scrambling to turn them into a political issue.
Cimoszewicz told parliament weather forecasts predicted heavy rain overnight.
"We must expect the possiblity, unfortunately, of the start of another wave of floods," he told an emergency session of parliament.
The prime minister said that as levels in rivers were still high and there was not much capacity in reservoirs, there was less scope to absorb additional water.

Police put the death toll in Poland by late Wednesday at 46 in the current wave of floods. Water has swamped 4,500 sq km (1,700 square miles), of which around two-fifths was still inundated. It has struck 40,000 farms, 86 towns and 875 villages.

While waters were slowly receding in the south, leaving a terrible stench and a risk of disease in communities shrouded in sewage, rubbish and dead animals, a wave of high water continued to advance northwards along the Odra river.
It reached areas of the German border and caused an evacuation of people from the border town of Slubice. Streets of Nowa Sol were swamped by the wave.
Parliament was discussing 22 laws designed to rush funds and aid to the hundreds of affected communities.
These include bills to change the current budget to allow more borrowing at home and abroad, rapid cash payments to affected households, and reserve grain supplies to farmers.

Opposition parties have heaped criticism on the government for its crisis handling, saying it did too little, too late and especially reproaching it for failing to call a state of emergency which could have yielded useful extra powers.
After Cimoszewicz's dramatic statement, pressure grew on the government in the lower house to do more.

The government has strongly defended its flood-fighting record, mindful the issue could bear strongly on the result of elections in which Cimoszewicz's Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) is challenged by a bloc led by the Solidarity union.
As the government faced a massive task of urgent relief and longer-term reconstruction, it walked a tightrope between the need for resources and a danger of harming economic stability.

The zloty slid five percent on Tuesday against a basket of foreign currencies and after partial recovery and stabilisation on Wednesday it showed signs of nervousness again in Warsaw on Thursday, despite reassuring comments from Finance Minister Marek Belka.

"It was not foreign investors, it seems, who were fleeing the zloty but domestic traders who went wild and began moving from zlotys to dollars," Belka told public radio on Thursday before Cimoszewicz's statement. "I watch it with calm...I think it will now reverse," he said.

To deal with the disaster's aftermath the government was seeking a 2.5 billion zloty ($710 million) credit line from the central bank and $300 million World Bank loan after it had already squeezed 650 million zlotys from exisiting budget resources.
